assignments.title: CotW Final Project
assignments.html:
CotW Final Project
7th Grade ELA · Module 2 · Week 6
40 points6 files, one submissionDue end of Week 6
The Call of the Wild: Your Final Project
 

Argumentative essay (about 500 to 700 words) + transformation visual + two-worlds scene + spoken explanation + reflection

Focus question
 
Does Buck's transformation set him free, or destroy who he was?
What you are making
 

Buck begins as the king of a warm, comfortable home and ends as a creature of the wild, running with the wolves. Readers disagree about what that change means. Some say the wild sets Buck free to become what he truly is. Others say it destroys the loyal, loving dog he once was.

Your project answers the focus question two ways. First, an argumentative essay: you have practiced it in Quick Writes 2, 3, 4, and 5 (a thesis, evidence with explanation, a counterclaim, and an outline with an introduction), and the Week 6 lessons take you from plan to polished essay. Second, a creative piece: a visual and a two-worlds scene that let a viewer see and hear the change. The Week 6 lessons coach both, and your Week 6 PDF holds that work.

The essay
 

Write an argumentative essay that answers the focus question. Take a clear position, state it as a thesis, support it with evidence from the book and explain that evidence, raise the strongest argument against your view and answer it, then close with a conclusion. Build it from your Quick Writes 2 to 5 and your Transformation Log, saved in your lesson PDFs in your OneDrive course folder. About 500 to 700 words, about 70 minutes of writing time, spread out.

1
Write your thesis.
Decide your position on the focus question: does the change set Buck free, or destroy who he was? Write one clear sentence that states your answer. This is your thesis. Put it at the end of a short opening paragraph that sets up the question.
2
Give your evidence and explain it.
Use two or three specific details or short quotations from the book that support your thesis. Cite each one in MLA format: London's last name plus the chapter, for example (London, Ch. 3). If you already name London in your sentence, just give the chapter. After each one, write a sentence or two that shows how it proves your point. Do not just drop the quotation; explain what it means. Pull these from your Quick Writes and your Transformation Log.
3
Raise a counterclaim and answer it.
Name the strongest argument someone on the other side would make. For example, if you argue the wild sets Buck free, a reader might point to how much he loves John Thornton. State that fairly in a sentence or two, then explain why your position still holds.
4
Write a conclusion.
End with two or three sentences that restate your thesis in fresh words and say what London wants readers to understand about instinct, survival, and the pull between civilization and the wild.
5
Add your Works Cited entry.
At the end of your document, add one entry for the novel: London, Jack. The Call of the Wild. 1903.
6
Be honest about your reasoning.
If a detail only partly fits, say so. Taking the other side seriously in your counterclaim makes your argument stronger, not weaker.
M365 skill step (the essay)

Before you submit, make sure you have:

☐Written in Microsoft Word, opened from your school M365 account.
☐Named your file LastName_CotW_FinalEssay (for example, Garcia_CotW_FinalEssay).
☐Set line spacing to double throughout the document.
☐Added your name, the course, and the date in the upper left, then centered a real title above your writing (MLA-style heading).
☐Used Heading styles for any section labels and a readable body font (Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12).
☐Saved it to your Optima > ELA > [your course folder] in OneDrive and confirmed it is there.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Applying Heading Styles (Word).

The creative piece
 

Buck starts as a pampered house dog in the sunny Santa Clara Valley and ends as a creature of the wild. Show that transformation two ways: a visual you create, and a two-worlds scene that sets his civilized world and the wild side by side.

A · Your transformation visual (choose one)

Create one visual that shows Buck's transformation from the tame house dog to the creature of the wild. Pick the format you like best:

›A "before and after" art piece, drawn by hand or made with any digital tool, showing Buck at Judge Miller's place beside Buck in the wild.
›A comic strip of three to six panels that shows the key moments of Buck's change.
›A map of Buck's journey from the Santa Clara Valley to the Northland, marking the places where he changes the most.

Whichever you choose, the transformation must be obvious, and your visual must point at the theme: that Buck is pulled between civilization and the wild, and the wild wins.

B · Two Worlds, One Frame
1
Make one scene with two sides: a single PowerPoint slide, a drawing, a collage, or a photograph of a small model you build.
2
On one side, Buck's civilized world: warm, comfortable objects that suggest the big house and easy living. On the other side, the wild: cold, open objects that suggest the Northland.
3
Between them, a path of three to five objects or moments that show the journey.
4
Add two labels, one per side, each one sentence naming who Buck is in that world.
5
Save it as an image or PDF named LastName_CotW_TwoWorlds.
6
Record a spoken explanation, 30 to 60 seconds: walk a viewer from Buck's civilized world to the wild, in order, and name the one key point your scene makes about the pull between civilization and the wild. Record it with PowerPoint's Record button, Canvas media recording, or a phone or laptop. This spoken part is required and graded for everyone.
C · Your reflection (200 to 250 words)

Write a reflection of 200 to 250 words in Word. Explain what you learned about Buck's transformation from building this contrast. What did placing the two worlds side by side show you that reading alone did not? How do the two sides help you understand the pull between civilization and the wild, and your answer to the focus question? Name it LastName_CotW_ProjectReflection and save it to your OneDrive course folder.

Success criteria
 
☐A clear thesis takes a position and answers the focus question.
☐Two or three pieces of evidence from the book, each cited in MLA format (author plus chapter), and each explained, not just quoted.
☐A counterclaim is raised fairly and answered.
☐A conclusion ties the argument back to the theme of civilization and the wild, and a Works Cited entry for the novel appears at the end of the essay.
☐The essay uses clear paragraphs and is checked for clear sentences and spelling.
☐The visual shows both Buck's tame world and the wild and makes the transformation obvious.
☐The two-worlds scene shows both sides, a path, and two labels.
☐The spoken explanation is 30 to 60 seconds, moves in order, and names one key point.
☐The reflection is 200 to 250 words and connects the contrast to the theme of civilization and the wild.
☐Everything is uploaded together, in one submission.
Submission
 

Upload everything here, in one submission:

1
Your Week 6 PDF (download it from the Turn In step at the end of Week 6 Lesson 4).
2
Your essay as a Word document (LastName_CotW_FinalEssay).
3
Your transformation visual.
4
Your two-worlds scene (LastName_CotW_TwoWorlds).
5
Your spoken explanation (a recording file, or record it here with Canvas media recording).
6
Your reflection as a Word document (LastName_CotW_ProjectReflection).

Due: end of Week 6. Then take the Week 6 Quiz.

You already did the thinking in your Quick Writes. This is where it comes together.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 1 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · Module 2 · Week 1
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 1 submissions before you move on:

☐Week 1 Work (one PDF)
☐This Week 1 Quiz

questions.text: Where does Buck live at the start of Chapter 1?

answers.text: On a fishing boat off Seattle.
In a kennel in the Klondike.
At Judge Miller's place in the Santa Clara Valley.
In a city apartment in San Francisco.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck rules Judge Miller's estate in the warm, sun-kissed Santa Clara Valley.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening pages. Buck's home is a large California estate.

questions.text: What kind of dog is Buck before he is taken away?

answers.text: A strong, proud dog who rules the estate and keeps his body hard with outdoor life.
A small, spoiled lapdog who never goes outside.
A wild dog that has never lived with people.
A sled dog already trained for the snow.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. London shows Buck as king of the estate, proud, and kept hard by hunting and swimming, not soft.
questions.feedback_incorrect: London is careful to say Buck is not a pampered house-dog. Hunting kept his muscles hard.

questions.text: How does Buck end up leaving the estate?

answers.text: The Judge sells him to a dog-doctor.
He runs away on his own.
He is lost during a hunt.
Manuel, a gardener's helper, secretly sells him for gambling money.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Manuel betrays Buck and sells him to a stranger to pay his gambling debts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the night of Manuel's treachery. A gardener's helper leads Buck away and sells him.

questions.text: After two days and nights in the express car, London says Buck was so changed "that the Judge himself would not have recognized him" (London, Ch. 1). What does this show?

answers.text: Buck has caught a disease.
The harsh treatment is already changing the kind of creature Buck is.
Buck has decided to obey everyone.
Buck is only pretending to be angry.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The cruelty, the hunger and the thirst of the trip are transforming the comfortable Buck into something fierce.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Even the Judge would not know him. The cruelty and hunger of the trip are remaking Buck.

questions.text: What lesson does the man in the red sweater teach Buck with the club?

answers.text: That Buck should always fight harder.
That men can never be trusted at all.
That a man with a club is a master to be obeyed.
That Buck is free to leave.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck sees that he stands no chance against a man with a club, so a man with a club is a master to be obeyed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the scene in the yard. The club shows Buck who holds power in this new world.

questions.text: In this line from Chapter 1, "Buck had accepted the rope" (London, Ch. 1), which word is the DIRECT object?

answers.text: Buck
accepted
had
rope

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "Buck accepted what?" The answer is rope, so rope is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the action verb, then ask "accepted what?" The answer is the direct object.

questions.text:
Which word is the INDIRECT object?

Example sentence: François gave Buck his supper.

answers.text: Buck
François
gave
supper

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The supper was given to Buck, so Buck is the indirect object. Supper is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: First find the direct object (supper), then ask "gave supper to whom?" The answer is the indirect object.

questions.text: A "dynamic character" is one who:

answers.text: appears in many scenes.
never speaks.
changes over the course of the story.
is always the hero.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Buck is a dynamic character. The events of the story change who he is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dynamic character changes through the story. Buck is the clearest example.

questions.text:
A direct object receives the action of the verb. Which word is the direct object?

Example sentence: Manuel doubled a rope around Buck's neck.

answers.text: Manuel
doubled
neck
rope

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "Manuel doubled what?" The answer is rope, so rope is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the action verb, then ask "Manuel doubled what?" The answer is the direct object.

questions.text: Which question finds the direct object?

answers.text: Subject verb to whom or for whom?
Subject verb what or whom?
What kind, which one, how many?
How, when, where, to what extent?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After the action verb, ask "what or whom?" to find the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The direct object answers "what or whom?" right after the action verb. "To whom or for whom" finds the indirect object.

questions.text:
Which word is the direct object?

Example sentence: He drank the water eagerly.

answers.text: eagerly
He
water
drank

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "He drank what?" The answer is water, so water is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the action verb drank, then ask "drank what?" The answer is the direct object.

questions.text:
An indirect object names the one the action is done to or for. Which word is the indirect object?

Example sentence: The man brought Buck water.

answers.text: Buck
water
man
brought

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The water was brought to Buck, so Buck is the indirect object. Water is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: First find the direct object (water), then ask "brought water to whom?" The answer is the indirect object.

questions.text: Which question finds the indirect object?

answers.text: Who or what verb?
Verb plus direct object, to whom or for whom?
What kind or which one?
How or when?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After you find the direct object, ask "to whom or for whom?" to find the indirect object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The indirect object answers "to whom or for whom?" once you already have the direct object.

questions.text:
Which word is the INDIRECT object?

Example sentence: Perrault paid the man three hundred dollars.

answers.text: Perrault
dollars
man
paid

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The dollars were paid to the man, so man is the indirect object. Dollars is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dollars is the direct object (paid what?). The man is who it was paid to, so the man is the indirect object.

questions.text:
Which word is the DIRECT object?

Example sentence: The North taught Buck a hard lesson.

answers.text: Buck
lesson
North
taught

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "taught what?" The answer is lesson, so lesson is the direct object. Buck is the indirect object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Buck is who the lesson was taught to (indirect object). The thing taught, the lesson, is the direct object.

questions.text: Which is true about indirect objects?

answers.text: A sentence can have an indirect object with no direct object.
The indirect object answers "how" or "when."
The indirect object always comes after the direct object.
You cannot have an indirect object without a direct object.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The indirect object names who the direct object is given to or done for, so there must be a direct object first.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The indirect object names who receives the direct object, so a direct object must be present. It also sits before the direct object, not after.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 2 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · Module 2 · Week 2
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 2 submissions before you move on:

☐Week 2 Work (one PDF)
☐This Week 2 Quiz

questions.text: What is "the law of club and fang" in Buck's new world?

answers.text: A set of rules the men teach the dogs in school.
The Southland code of fairness and trust.
The brutal code where the man with the club gives orders and the strongest dog wins.
The rule that only the lead dog may punish the others.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The club is the men's power and the fang is the dogs' power. In the Northland there is no other law.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening of Chapter 2. The club belongs to the men, the fang to the dogs, and there is no fair play.

questions.text: What lesson does Buck take from what happens to Curly on the Dyea beach?

answers.text: Never go down, because a fallen dog is finished.
Friendly dogs are always safe.
The men will always protect the dogs.
Fights are settled fairly, one on one.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Buck sees there is no fair play and once a dog is down, it is over. He vows never to go down.
questions.feedback_incorrect: After Curly falls, the pack closes in and no one saves her. Buck's lesson is to never be the one who goes down.

questions.text: Which is the best example of Buck ADAPTING to survive in Chapter 2?

answers.text: He refuses to pull the sled.
He sleeps in the warm tent every night.
He shares his food with the other dogs.
He learns to eat fast and steal so his ration is not stolen first.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London calls this his adaptability, his capacity to adjust to changing conditions.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Adapting means changing to survive. Buck learns to eat fast and steal, the opposite of his old, fussy habits.

questions.text: Tone is best described as:

answers.text: The order in which events happen.
The author's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice.
The number of characters in a chapter.
The feeling a scene gives the reader.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Tone is the writer's attitude, built mostly through the words the author chooses. The feeling a scene gives you as a reader is mood.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Tone is not the events, and it is not the feeling you get as a reader (that is mood). It is the author's attitude, shown through word choice.

questions.text: London writes that "a chill wind was blowing that nipped him sharply" (London, Ch. 2). Which word does the most to make the wind feel like an attacker?

answers.text: chill
blowing
nipped
wind

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Wind cannot really nip, so nipped turns the cold into a creature that bites. A milder word like touched would soften the whole tone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that makes the wind act like an animal. Nipped makes the cold feel like one more enemy Buck has to survive.

questions.text: Which sentence has a TRANSITIVE verb (a verb with a receiver)?

answers.text: The dogs rested by the sled.
Billee whined all night.
The wind blew from the north.
François lit a fire on the ice.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Lit what? A fire. The fire receives the action, so lit is transitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask each verb "whom or what?" Only lit has an answer: a fire. The other verbs have no receiver.

questions.text: Which sentence places its commas correctly?

answers.text: By morning, the snow had buried Buck completely.
By morning the snow had buried Buck, completely.
By, morning the snow had buried Buck completely.
By morning the snow, had buried Buck completely.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The introductory phrase By morning is followed by a comma, and no comma interrupts the main sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The comma belongs after the introductory phrase By morning, not inside the main sentence.

questions.text: Which of these works best as a THESIS for an essay about Buck?

answers.text: Buck is harnessed to a sled in Chapter 2.
Does Buck change for the better?
Buck gains strength and cunning in the Northland, but he loses the trust and fairness of his old self.
Buck changes a lot in the Northland.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It makes a clear, specific, arguable claim you could defend from the text. That is a thesis.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A thesis takes a specific, arguable side. A fact, a question, or a vague statement will not work as one.

questions.text: A transitive verb passes its action to a receiver. What question finds that receiver?

answers.text: How? When? Where?
Who or what does the action?
Whose is it?
The verb plus "whom?" or "what?"

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After the action verb, ask "whom?" or "what?" If the sentence answers, the verb is transitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To find a receiver, ask the verb "whom?" or "what?" The "how, when, where" questions belong to adverbs.

questions.text:
Is the verb transitive or intransitive?

Example sentence: Pike slyly stole a slice of bacon.

answers.text: Intransitive, because there is no receiver.
Transitive, because "stole what?" has an answer: a slice of bacon.
Transitive, because slyly is the receiver.
Intransitive, because stole cannot take an object.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Stole what? A slice of bacon. The action lands on a receiver, so stole is transitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "stole what?" The sentence answers: a slice of bacon. That receiver makes the verb transitive.

questions.text: London writes, "Buck toiled in the traces" (London, Ch. 2). Is the verb transitive or intransitive?

answers.text: Transitive, because the traces is the receiver.
Transitive, because in points to a receiver.
Intransitive, because "toiled whom or what?" has no answer.
Intransitive, because toiled is a linking verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Toiled whom or what? Nothing answers. In the traces tells where, not what, so toiled is intransitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "toiled whom or what?" There is no receiver. In the traces tells where. So the verb is intransitive.

questions.text: In which example sentence is the bold verb intransitive (no receiver)?

answers.text: Every night the wind howled across the camp.
He bit the ice from his toes.
Buck hauled the sled.
Pike stole the bacon.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Howled whom or what? Nothing answers. Across the camp tells where, so howled is intransitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Test each verb with "whom or what?" Howled has no receiver. The others all do.

questions.text: A comma separates items in a series of three or more. Which example sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: Buck learned to haul, to obey and, to steal.
Buck learned to haul, to obey, and to steal.
Buck learned to haul to obey and to steal.
Buck, learned to haul, to obey, and to steal.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Three items in a series each get a comma, including before the and.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In a series of three, put a comma after each item before the final and: to haul, to obey, and to steal.

questions.text: Use a comma after an introductory word or phrase. Which example sentence is correct?

answers.text: By evening Perrault, secured another dog.
By, evening Perrault secured another dog.
By evening, Perrault secured another dog.
By evening Perrault secured, another dog.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The introductory phrase By evening is followed by a comma before the main sentence begins.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The comma goes right after the introductory phrase By evening, not inside the main sentence.

questions.text:
Why are there commas around the lead dog?

Example sentence: Spitz, the lead dog, ran out his tongue and laughed.

answers.text: It begins a new sentence.
It is an interrupter that renames Spitz and could be lifted out.
It is a series of three items.
It is the receiver of the verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The lead dog renames Spitz and could be removed without breaking the sentence, so commas set it off on both sides.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The lead dog simply renames Spitz. You could lift it out and the sentence still works, so a pair of commas sets it off.

questions.text: Which example sentence places ALL its commas correctly?

answers.text: Cold, hungry, and tired Buck dug a nest in the snow.
Cold hungry and tired, Buck dug a nest in the snow.
Cold, hungry and tired, Buck, dug a nest in the snow.
Cold, hungry, and tired, Buck dug a nest in the snow.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The three describing words form a series, and the whole introductory group is closed off with a comma before Buck.
questions.feedback_incorrect: You need commas between the three describing words and one more comma after the introductory group, before Buck.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 3 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · Module 2 · Week 3
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 3 submissions before you move on:

☐Week 3 Work (one PDF)
☐This Week 3 Quiz

questions.text: What finally makes Buck attack Spitz for the first time, at the camp on Lake Le Barge?

answers.text: Spitz steals Buck's food during a meal.
Spitz attacks François.
Spitz takes over Buck's warm sleeping nest.
Spitz refuses to pull the sled.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. When Buck returns and finds Spitz in his nest, "the beast in him roared," and he springs at Spitz.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the camp scene at Lake Le Barge. The trigger is about Buck's nest.

questions.text: London calls the wild, ancient nature growing in Buck "the dominant primordial beast" (London, Ch. 3). What does this mean?

answers.text: The old, wild instincts of Buck's ancestors are taking charge in him.
Buck is turning into an actual wolf overnight.
Buck has caught a disease from the other dogs.
Buck is the largest dog on the team.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The primordial beast is the ancient, wild side of Buck's nature, growing stronger under trail life.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Primordial means belonging to the earliest, most ancient stage. The phrase names Buck's reawakening wild instincts.

questions.text: How does Buck finally beat Spitz in their fight to the death?

answers.text: The other dogs help him.
François pulls Spitz away.
Spitz gives up and runs.
He fights by head as well as by instinct and uses a trick that leaves Spitz unable to stand.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London says, "He fought by instinct, but he could fight by head as well." Buck wins with a trick, and Spitz cannot stand. He uses imagination, not just instinct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the line "He fought by instinct, but he could fight by head as well." Buck wins by thinking, with a trick, not only by fury.

questions.text: Which line from Chapter 3 is an example of a SIMILE?

answers.text: "The beast in him roared."
"a wind that cut like a white-hot knife"
"the dominant primordial beast"
"Mercy was a thing reserved for gentler climes."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The word like compares the wind to a white-hot knife. That is a simile.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A simile uses like or as to compare two things. Find the line with one of those words.

questions.text: London writes of "the pride that laid hold of them at break of camp" (London, Ch. 3). Giving pride, a feeling, the power to lay hold of the dogs is:

answers.text: a simile
a fragment
personification
a run-on

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Pride is a feeling, but London lets it grab hold of the dogs like a living thing. That is personification.
questions.feedback_incorrect: There is no like or as, so it is not a simile. Pride is a feeling, yet London gives it a living thing's action. Giving non-human things human qualities is personification.

questions.text: Which group of words is a complete COMPLEX sentence?

answers.text: Because the beast in him roared.
The two dogs snarling in the moonlight.
Buck won the fight the team grew calm.
After the team reached Lake Le Barge, the men made camp.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It joins a dependent clause (After the team reached Lake Le Barge) with an independent clause, correctly punctuated.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence has one dependent clause and one independent clause. Find the complete one.

questions.text: Which example sentence is a RUN-ON that needs to be fixed?

answers.text: The snow fell all night the dogs slept under it.
The snow fell all night. The dogs slept under it.
While the snow fell all night, the dogs slept under it.
The snow fell all night, and the dogs slept under it.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete thoughts are jammed together with nothing between them. That is a run-on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on crowds two complete thoughts together with no period, semicolon, or comma plus conjunction. Find that one.

questions.text: In an argument, after you state a claim and give a quote, what is the job of your EXPLANATION?

answers.text: To add a second quote.
To summarize the whole chapter.
To explain why the quote proves your claim and answer "so what?"
To state your opinion with no evidence.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The explanation connects the quote back to your claim and shows the reader why it matters.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The explanation is where you tie the quote to your claim and answer "so what?" It is what makes the evidence count.

questions.text: A clause that has a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence is called:

answers.text: a dependent clause
a fragment
a phrase
an independent clause

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. An independent clause is a complete thought and can stand by itself.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The clause that can stand alone as a full sentence is the independent clause.

questions.text: In this sentence, "When Buck finished his ration and returned, he found his nest occupied" (London, Ch. 3), which part is the dependent clause?

answers.text: he found his nest occupied
When Buck finished his ration and returned
his nest occupied
Buck finished

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The word When makes that part lean on the rest, so it cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The part that starts with When leaves you waiting. That is the dependent clause.

questions.text: A complex sentence is made of:

answers.text: two independent clauses
two dependent clauses
one independent clause and one dependent clause
one phrase and one word

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A complex sentence joins one independent clause with one dependent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence pairs one clause that can stand alone with one that cannot.

questions.text: Which group of words is a sentence FRAGMENT, not a complete sentence?

answers.text: Because Spitz had stolen his warm nest.
The beast in him roared.
Buck sprang upon Spitz.
Spitz was a practised fighter.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It has a subject and verb, but Because makes it depend on more. Standing alone, it is a fragment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the choice that starts with a conjunction and leaves the thought unfinished.

questions.text:
What is the best way to FIX this fragment?

Example fragment: Because Spitz had stolen his warm nest.

answers.text: Add a comma at the end.
Join it to a complete thought: Because Spitz had stolen his warm nest, Buck attacked.
Capitalize the first word.
Delete the word Because and leave it as is.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Attaching the dependent clause to an independent clause makes a complete complex sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A fragment needs to be joined to a complete thought, not just repunctuated.

questions.text: A RUN-ON sentence is best described as:

answers.text: a sentence that is too short
a sentence with too many adjectives
two complete thoughts jammed together without correct punctuation or a joining word
a clause that cannot stand alone

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A run-on crowds two complete thoughts together with no period, semicolon, or conjunction to join them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on is two complete thoughts pushed together without correct punctuation or a joining word.

questions.text: Which example sentence is a RUN-ON?

answers.text: Buck won the fight, and the team grew calm.
Spitz was beaten Buck became the leader.
After Spitz was beaten, Buck became the leader.
Spitz was beaten. Buck became the leader.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete thoughts are jammed together with nothing between them. That is a run-on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the choice where two full sentences run together with no period, comma and conjunction, or semicolon.

questions.text:
Which is a correct way to FIX this run-on?

Example run-on: Spitz was beaten Buck became the leader.

answers.text: Spitz was beaten, Buck became the leader.
Spitz was beaten Buck, became the leader.
Spitz, was beaten Buck became the leader.
Spitz was beaten. Buck became the leader.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Splitting the run-on into two complete sentences with a period is one correct fix. A semicolon or a comma plus a conjunction would also work.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on is fixed with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word. A comma alone is not enough.

quizzes.title: Week 4 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 4 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · Module 2 · Week 4
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 4 submissions before you move on:

☐Week 4 Work (one PDF)
☐This Week 4 Quiz

questions.text: In Chapter 4, how does Buck finally get the lead position on the team?

answers.text: François rewards him for good behavior.
Dave, the wheel dog, steps aside and lets him lead.
He refuses every other place until the men give in and let him lead.
Perrault trades him for two new dogs.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck will not take any place but the front, circling the camp for nearly an hour until the men let him lead.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the morning after the Spitz fight. Buck demands the lead and refuses every lesser place.

questions.text: After he takes the lead, how does Buck prove he has earned it?

answers.text: He makes the loafers pull, disciplines the team, and breaks in new dogs fast.
He stops working and rests by the fire.
He runs away from the team.
He lets the other dogs do whatever they want.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck makes Pike pull, punishes Joe, and breaks in Teek and Koona so fast it takes the driver's breath away.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at what Buck does on the trail once he leads. He whips the team into shape and proves his mastery.

questions.text: Why does the sick dog Dave fight to stay in the harness even though it is killing him?

answers.text: He is afraid of the other dogs.
He wants to escape the trail.
He does not understand he is hurt.
His pride in the work of the trail is his whole life, and he cannot bear another dog doing his job.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The work is who Dave is. Taken out of the team, he bites through Sol-leks's traces to stand in his own place.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the part where Dave bites through Sol-leks's traces. His pride in the work is the reason.

questions.text: What is the main difference between the skilled drivers and the new owners, Hal, Charles, and Mercedes?

answers.text: The skilled drivers had more money.
The skilled drivers knew the trail and cared for the dogs; the new owners did not know how to work dogs or themselves.
The new owners had better dogs.
The skilled drivers traveled in summer only.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. On the mail trail the drivers saw to the dogs first every night (Ch. 4). Hal, Charles, and Mercedes did not know how to work dogs, or themselves (Ch. 5).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Compare how each group treated the dogs and the trail. The difference is knowledge and judgment.

questions.text: Which detail best shows the toil and cruelty of the trail in Chapter 5?

answers.text: The dogs are well fed and rested.
The drivers ride in a heated sled.
The dogs become "perambulating skeletons" (London, Ch. 5), so worn that the bite of the whip feels dull and distant.
The team makes a cheerful, easy journey.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London describes the dogs as walking skeletons, too exhausted to feel the lash. That is the toil of the trail.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the description of how worn down the starving dogs become. The toil is in those harsh details.

questions.text: At the end of Chapter 5, why does John Thornton cut Buck loose from the team?

answers.text: Hal asks him to buy Buck.
Buck has won a fight.
The team needs one fewer dog.
Buck senses danger on the rotten ice ahead and will not get up, Hal beats him, and Thornton stops Hal to save Buck.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck "sensed disaster close at hand, out there ahead on the ice where his master was trying to drive him." Thornton stops the beating and cuts Buck's traces, saving his life.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the moment Buck will not get up and Thornton stops the beating. Buck's instinct senses the danger.

questions.text: In a strong argument, a counterclaim is best described as:

answers.text: the strongest fair point against your claim, which you then answer
a repeat of your own claim
a list of all your evidence
the very first sentence of the essay

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A counterclaim names the strongest fair opposing point, and then you answer it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A counterclaim states the OTHER side fairly, then you answer it. It is not a repeat of your own claim.

questions.text:
Which mark correctly fills the blank?

Example sentence: The dogs were tired ___ the drivers were grumbling.

answers.text: a colon, because a list follows
a comma, because the two parts are short
a semicolon, because a complete sentence follows
no mark is needed

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The drivers were grumbling is a complete sentence, so a semicolon joins the two closely related sentences.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at what comes after the blank. It is a complete sentence, so the join is a semicolon.

questions.text: A colon is used correctly when:

answers.text: it joins two complete sentences of equal weight
it separates items inside a list
it replaces every comma in a long sentence
a complete sentence comes before it and a list or explanation follows

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A colon follows a complete sentence and points ahead to a list or an explanation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it and points ahead to a list or explanation.

questions.text: Which example sentence uses the colon correctly?

answers.text: The dogs that remained were: Joe, Pike, and Buck.
Five dogs remained: Joe, Pike, Sol-leks, Teek, and Buck.
Five dogs: remained Joe, Pike, and Buck.
Five dogs remained Joe, Pike: and Buck.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Five dogs remained is a complete sentence, so the colon can point ahead to the list.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the words before the colon. They must form a complete sentence, like Five dogs remained.

questions.text: Which example sentence correctly uses a semicolon?

answers.text: Because the trail was long; the dogs grew tired.
The owners packed: a tent, dishes, and canned goods.
The sled was overloaded; the dogs could not move it.
Hal whipped the dogs; and Mercedes wept.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A complete sentence sits on each side, so the semicolon joins them correctly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, with no joining word like and after it.

questions.text: Which example sentence correctly uses a conjunctive adverb?

answers.text: The sled was overloaded; however, the dogs still tried to pull it.
The trail was long, however the dogs kept moving.
The sled was overloaded; however the dogs still tried to pull it.
However the sled was overloaded, the dogs kept pulling.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A semicolon comes before the conjunctive adverb, and a comma comes right after it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the punctuation around however. It needs a semicolon before it and a comma right after it.

questions.text: Correlative conjunctions are conjunctions that:

answers.text: always end in -ly
come in pairs, with both parts working together
can only join two nouns
replace a subject pronoun

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Correlative conjunctions come in pairs, like either...or and not only...but also.
questions.feedback_incorrect: They work in pairs. Think of either...or or both...and.

questions.text:
Which word completes the correlative pair?

Example sentence: Neither the dogs ___ the people noticed the spring.

answers.text: or
but
nor
and

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Neither always pairs with nor.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Neither has one fixed partner. It is nor.

questions.text: Which example sentence uses a correlative conjunction pair correctly?

answers.text: Both Charles or Hal believed he worked hardest.
Not only did they fail to work the dogs, but they failed to work themselves.
The team would neither pull and stop.
Either the ice was rotten nor the trail was safe.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Not only...but is a correct correlative pair joining two ideas.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Match the partners: both...and, either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also.

questions.text:
Which correlative pair best completes the example sentence?

Example sentence: Buck would ___ take the lead ___ accept any lesser place.

answers.text: both...and
neither...but
not only...nor
either...or

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Either...or presents two choices, which fits Buck taking the lead or refusing every other spot.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The sentence offers two choices. The pair that presents a choice is either...or.

quizzes.title: Week 5 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 5 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · Module 2 · Week 5
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 5 submissions before you move on:

☐Week 5 Work (one PDF)
☐This Week 5 Quiz

questions.text: Who is John Thornton, and why does he matter to Buck in Chapter 6?

answers.text: A cruel driver who beats Buck.
Another sled dog on the team.
The man who saved Buck's life from Hal's club, and the first person Buck truly loves.
The judge who first owned Buck in California.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Thornton cut Buck free at the end of Chapter 5, and in Chapter 6 Buck feels true love for the first time.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening of Chapter 6: "This man had saved his life, which was something; but, further, he was the ideal master."

questions.text: London writes that the call lured Buck into the forest, but "the love for John Thornton drew him back to the fire again" (London, Ch. 6). What does this show?

answers.text: Two forces are pulling on Buck at the same time, and the love pulls him back.
Buck no longer feels the call of the wild at all.
Buck has fully become a wild wolf.
Thornton wants Buck to leave.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The wild pulls Buck toward the forest, and his love for Thornton pulls him back. He is caught between the two.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Notice that both forces act on Buck. The call pulls one way; the love pulls the other.

questions.text: Which detail shows that Buck is still wild even while he loves Thornton?

answers.text: Buck lies at Thornton's feet for hours.
Buck lets Skeet clean his wounds.
Buck follows Thornton out of the tent.
Buck shows no mercy to strange dogs and still hears the wild call.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck fights other dogs without mercy and still feels the call, proof the wild is alive in him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the moment that shows the primitive, not the tame. The love details show the opposite.

questions.text: Why does Buck attack "Black" Burton in the saloon?

answers.text: Burton steals Buck's food.
Burton strikes John Thornton.
Burton is another sled driver.
Buck wants to leave the camp.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The moment Burton hits Thornton, Buck leaps at him. His love drives him to protect his master.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the saloon scene. Buck moves the instant someone hurts Thornton.

questions.text: This week's poem tells a grim story but feels lively and even funny. Which part of the poem's FORM creates that feeling?

answers.text: Its long, plain sentences with no pattern.
Its lack of any characters.
Its swinging beat and chiming rhymes.
Its missing ending.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The bouncy beat and the rhymes give a dark story a wild, almost cheerful energy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what made the poem fun to say aloud. The beat and the rhyme shape the tone.

questions.text: The poem ends by repeating its whole opening stanza (the frame). What is the job of that returning stanza?

answers.text: It hides the poem's meaning.
It ends the poem early.
It tells the reader to stop.
It works like a song's chorus, bringing the tale back to where it began and driving home its main feeling.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Like a song's chorus, the returning stanza closes the frame and presses the main feeling on the reader.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think of a song. The part that comes back, the chorus, is what sticks and carries the feeling.

questions.text: Which phrase uses a NOUN to do an adjective's job?

answers.text: a freight sled
a heavy sled
a long sled
a wooden sled

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Freight is a noun (the goods a sled carries), and here it tells what kind of sled.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Heavy, long and wooden are adjectives already. Look for the word that is usually a noun but here tells what kind of sled.

questions.text: Which example sentence should end with a question mark?

answers.text: Matthewson asked whether Buck could start a thousand pounds
Thornton wondered how heavy the load was
Do you think Buck can start a thousand pounds
The crowd waited to see if the sled would move

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It asks a question directly, so it ends with a question mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The other three only report that someone asked or wondered. A sentence that tells about a question ends with a period.

questions.text: Sometimes a noun stands in front of another noun and describes it. Which word is the noun doing an adjective's job in the phrase a river bank?

answers.text: river
bank
a

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. River tells what kind of bank, so the noun river is doing an adjective's job.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "what kind of bank?" The word that answers is the noun doing the adjective's job.

questions.text: In the phrase "love names" (London, Ch. 6), which word is being described (the main noun)?

answers.text: love
names

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Names is the main noun. Love is the noun in front of it, telling what kind.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The main noun is the real thing being talked about. Love is only describing it.

questions.text: A noun is doing an adjective's job when it answers which questions about the noun beside it?

answers.text: How? When? Where?
To what extent?
What kind? Which one?

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Like any adjective, it answers "what kind" or "which one" about a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "How, when, where" belong to adverbs. A noun doing an adjective's job answers "what kind" or "which one."

questions.text:
Which mark joins two complete sentences that are closely related, without a conjunction?

Example sentence: Buck loved Thornton fiercely ___ he still heard the wild call.

answers.text: a semicolon
a comma
a colon
a question mark

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both sides are complete sentences, so a semicolon joins them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each side can stand alone as a sentence. The mark that joins two complete sentences is the semicolon.

questions.text:
Which mark says "here it comes" and introduces a list after a complete sentence?

Example sentence: Three dogs loafed by the river ___ Buck, Skeet, and Nig.

answers.text: a semicolon
a colon
a comma

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A colon introduces the list that follows the complete sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The blank comes right before a list. The mark that introduces a list is the colon.

questions.text: Which example sentence uses commas correctly to separate items in a list?

answers.text: Skeet Nig and Buck romped together.
Skeet; Nig; and Buck romped together.
Skeet, Nig, and Buck romped together.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Commas separate the items in a list.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Items in a simple list are separated by commas, not semicolons or nothing at all.

questions.text:
Thornton shouts an urgent command above the rapids. Which end mark best fits the blank?

Go, Buck ___

answers.text: a period
an exclamation point
a comma

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A shouted, urgent command takes an exclamation point, as in London's line: "Go, Buck! Go!" (London, Ch. 6).
questions.feedback_incorrect: He is shouting an urgent command. The end mark for a strong cry is the exclamation point.

questions.text: Which example sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: This man had saved his life; he was the ideal master.
This man had saved his life, he was the ideal master.
This man had saved his life: he was, the ideal master.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete sentences joined without a conjunction need a semicolon, not a comma.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Joining two complete sentences with only a comma is a run-on. Use a semicolon between them.

quizzes.title: Week 6 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 6 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · Module 2 · Week 6
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 6 submissions before you move on:

☐CotW Final Project (your Week 6 PDF, your essay, and your creative files)
☐This Week 6 Quiz

questions.text: Why do John Thornton and his partners travel into the East at the start of Chapter 7?

answers.text: To deliver the mail to Dawson.
To take Buck back to the Santa Clara Valley.
To search for a fabled lost mine that many men had sought.
To sell their dogs to the gold miners.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The money Buck won lets Thornton pay off his debts and go after a lost mine "as old as the history of the country" (London, Ch. 7).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 7. The journey is a treasure hunt.

questions.text: London says John Thornton "was unafraid of the wild" (London, Ch. 7). What does Thornton need to travel through the wilderness?

answers.text: A handful of salt and a rifle; he hunts his dinner as he goes.
A full sled of canned food and tents.
A guide who knows the trail.
A map of the Lost Cabin.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Thornton asks little of man or nature. He travels light and lives on what he hunts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: London shows Thornton at home in the wild. He carries almost nothing and hunts along the way.

questions.text: By the fire, Buck has visions of a short-legged hairy man. What does London say seems to be the main feeling of that other world?

answers.text: Joy
Hunger
Loneliness
Fear

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London writes, "The salient thing of this other world seemed fear" (London, Ch. 7). The hairy man sleeps restlessly and watches for danger.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at how the hairy man sleeps and moves: he starts awake and peers into the darkness. Name that feeling.

questions.text: When Buck first meets the timber wolf, what happens?

answers.text: The wolf attacks Buck, and they fight until the wolf gives up.
The wolf runs; Buck chases him, corners him without attacking, and they finally sniff noses and become friends.
The wolf calls the pack, and Buck runs back to camp.
Buck ignores the wolf and keeps hunting.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Buck keeps making friendly advances until the wolf sees no harm is meant. Then they run side by side.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the chase in the creek bed. Buck does not attack; he wants the wolf's company.

questions.text: Buck crosses the divide and wanders for a week in the land of timber and streams. What is he looking for?

answers.text: The Lost Cabin.
A way back to Dawson.
Fresh sign of the wild brother.
Thornton's partners.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He seeks "vainly for fresh sign of the wild brother" (London, Ch. 7), living on what he kills as he travels.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about who Buck ran with before he turned back. That is who he is hoping to find again.

questions.text: Why is the great bull moose in such a savage temper when Buck finds him?

answers.text: Buck has already bitten him.
He has lost his herd in a storm.
He is starving after a hard winter.
A feathered arrow-end sticks out of his side.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The arrow wound "accounted for his savageness" (London, Ch. 7).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the detail London gives just after he describes the bull's antlers. Something is already hurting him.

questions.text: London compares Buck to "the spider in its web, the snake in its coils, the panther in its ambuscade" (London, Ch. 7). What does this comparison show about Buck on the hunt?

answers.text: He has the patient, tireless waiting of a wild hunter.
He is afraid of the moose and hides from it.
He is tired and wants to rest.
He hunts the way Thornton taught him.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London calls it "a patience of the wild": Buck can hold on for hours, like other creatures that hunt their food.
questions.feedback_incorrect: All three animals wait, still and alert, for their prey. The comparison is about patience.

questions.text: At the moonlit clearing, when does the call come to Buck "in unmistakable accents" (London, Ch. 7)?

answers.text: When Buck first hears the yelps far away.
When the boldest wolf leaps at him.
After an old wolf sits, points his nose at the moon, and howls, and the others howl with him.
When the Yeehat people flee the camp.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The old wolf breaks out the long wolf howl, the pack joins, and Buck sits down and howls too.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the end of the clearing scene. A howl from the pack comes first, then Buck answers it.

questions.text: Which example sentence is a COMMA SPLICE?

answers.text: The partners washed the gravel; the gold piled up outside the lodge.
The partners washed the gravel, and the gold piled up outside the lodge.
As the partners washed the gravel, the gold piled up outside the lodge.
The partners washed the gravel, the gold piled up outside the lodge.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete sentences are joined with only a comma. That is a comma splice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with a comma alone. Find the one with no semicolon and no joining word.

questions.text:
Which is the correct fix for this run-on?

Example run-on: Thornton found an old flint-lock gun no one knew who had left it.

answers.text: Thornton found an old flint-lock gun, no one knew who had left it.
Thornton found an old flint-lock gun; no one knew who had left it.
Thornton found an old flint-lock gun no one, knew who had left it.
Thornton found an old flint-lock. Gun no one knew who had left it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A semicolon joins two complete sentences that belong together. A period or a comma plus and would also work.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A comma alone makes a comma splice. Put a semicolon, a period, or a comma and a joining word between the two complete sentences.

questions.text: Which group of words is a FRAGMENT?

answers.text: The call sounded again in the forest.
When the call sounded again, Buck left camp.
Because the call sounded again in the forest.
The call sounded again, so Buck left camp.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Because leaves the thought unfinished. It needs a complete sentence joined to it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A fragment is half a sentence. Look for the group of words that leaves you waiting for the rest.

questions.text: Which sentence punctuates the quotation and citation correctly?

answers.text: London says the call gave Buck "a vague, sweet gladness" (Ch. 7).
London says the call gave Buck "a vague, sweet gladness." (Ch. 7)
London says the call gave Buck "a vague, sweet gladness" (Ch. 7.)
London says the call gave Buck a vague, sweet gladness (London, Ch. 7).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The citation comes after the closing quotation mark, and the period comes after the citation. London is named in the sentence, so the chapter is enough.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Put the citation after the closing quotation mark and the period after the citation. London's exact words also need quotation marks.

questions.text: London writes, "To Buck it was boundless delight, this hunting, fishing, and indefinite wandering through strange places" (London, Ch. 7). A student wants to cut the middle. Which quotation does it honestly?

answers.text: "To Buck it was boundless delight wandering through strange places" (London, Ch. 7).
"To Buck it was boundless delight . . . wandering through strange places" (London, Ch. 7).
"To Buck it was a joy, wandering through strange places" (London, Ch. 7).
"To Buck it was boundless delight" . . . wandering through strange places (London, Ch. 7).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Three dots inside the quotation marks show exactly where words were cut, and every word that stays is London's.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When you cut words from the middle, three dots must mark the gap, inside the quotation, and no word may change.

questions.text: London writes, "Buck spent long hours musing by the fire" (London, Ch. 7). Which student sentence quotes him honestly?

answers.text: In Chapter 7, Buck "spent long hours dreaming by the fire" (London, Ch. 7).
In Chapter 7, Buck "spent hours musing by the fire" (London, Ch. 7).
In Chapter 7, Buck "spent long hours musing by the fire" (London, Ch. 7).
In Chapter 7, Buck "spent long, lazy hours musing by the fire" (London, Ch. 7).

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Every word inside the quotation marks is London's, in London's order.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each choice word for word. One changes a word, one drops a word without dots, and one adds a word.

questions.text: Paragraph 1 of an essay argues that Buck still loves Thornton. Paragraph 2 argues that the call wins in the end. Which sentence best begins Paragraph 2?

answers.text: Also, Buck is a dog.
Still, love cannot hold Buck forever, and Chapter 7 shows the call winning.
In conclusion, Buck loves Thornton.
The next paragraph is about the call.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It links the two paragraphs: it names the love from Paragraph 1 and turns toward the call.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A transition shows how two paragraphs connect. Choose the sentence that points back to the love and ahead to the call.

questions.text: Which example sentence punctuates Pete's words correctly?

answers.text: Pete said "when he was made, the mould was broke."
Pete said, "When he was made, the mould was broke".
Pete said, When he was made, the mould was broke.
Pete said, "When he was made, the mould was broke."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A comma comes before the quotation, the first spoken word takes a capital, and the period goes inside the closing mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check three things: a comma before the quotation, a capital on the first spoken word, and the period inside the closing mark.
